chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: smaller units first, then tenths and hundredths as parts of a unit, then the decimal point as a way of writing them, then comparing and computing. Every decimal rule is reached from the fractions the student already knows.

points.title: Try first, name later
points.text: The hook video leaves Sonu's two screws unmeasured. The tenth, the hundredth and the decimal point arrive only after the student has met a gap that a whole mark cannot name.

points.title: Fractions underneath every decimal
points.text: A decimal is a count of tenths, hundredths or thousandths. Adding, subtracting and comparing decimals use the same place value moves as whole numbers, so nothing is a trick to remember.

points.title: One zoom per digit
points.text: On the number line each digit names one more zoom into ten equal parts, and the end marks of a line decide what one division is worth.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic with one video per concept and a practice concept at the end; interactive tools appear only where handling the numbers is the idea. The book's questions follow in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

concepts.concept_name: Two screws that look the same

content.text:
3.1 The Need for Smaller Units
Sonu's mother was fixing a toy. She was trying to join two pieces with the help of a screw. Sonu was watching his mother with great curiosity. His mother was unable to join the pieces. Sonu asked why. His mother said that the screw was not of the right size.
She brought another screw from the box and was able to fix the toy.
The two screws looked the same to Sonu. But when he observed them closely, he saw they were of slightly different lengths.
Sonu was fascinated by how such a small difference in lengths could matter so much. He was curious to know the difference in lengths. He was also curious to know how little the difference was because the screws looked nearly the same.

concepts.concept_name: Reading between the marks

content.text:
As seen on the ruler, the unit length between two consecutive numbers is divided into 10 equal parts. To get the length 2 7/10 cm, we go from 0 to 2 and then take seven parts of 1/10. The length of the screw is 2 cm and 7/10 cm. Similarly, we can make sense of the length 3 2/10 cm.
We read 2 7/10 cm as two and seven-tenth centimeters, and 3 2/10 cm as three and two-tenth centimeters.
Can you explain why the unit was divided into smaller parts to measure the screws?

content.text:
1. Predict first: a screw ends after the 2 cm mark but before the 3 cm mark. Is it nearer 2 cm or 3 cm, and can a whole number of centimetres name its length?
2. No whole number fits, so the centimetre is split into 10 equal parts. Each part is 1/10 of a centimetre.
3. Count the whole centimetres first, then the tenths after them: that is how 2 7/10 cm is read.
4. Now measure a pen, a sharpener and one object of your choice, and write each length as units and tenths.

content.text:
Worked example: A ruler has every centimetre split into 10 equal parts. One screw ends 7 parts after the 2 cm mark and another ends 2 parts after the 3 cm mark. Write each length and say what the first one means.
1. The first screw is more than 2 1/2 cm but less than 3 cm, so it lies between 2 cm and 3 cm.
2. The unit between two consecutive numbers is divided into 10 equal parts, so each part is 1/10 cm.
3. From 0 we go to 2, then take 7 parts of 1/10: the length is 2 cm and 7/10 cm, that is 2 7/10 cm.
4. In the same way the second screw is 3 cm and 2/10 cm, that is 3 2/10 cm.
Answer: First screw 2 7/10 cm, second screw 3 2/10 cm

concepts.concept_name: Reading between the marks

content.text:
Worked example: Along a ruler marked in tenths of a centimetre, an eraser ends 4 parts after the 2 cm mark, a pencil ends 5 parts after the 4 cm mark and a chalk ends 4 parts after the 1 cm mark. Write each length.
1. Each part is 1/10 cm, so we read units first and then the parts.
2. Eraser: 2 cm and 4 parts, so 2 4/10 cm.
3. Pencil: 4 cm and 5 parts, so 4 5/10 cm, which is also 4 1/2 cm because 5/10 is half.
4. Chalk: 1 cm and 4 parts, so 1 4/10 cm.
Answer: Eraser 2 4/10 cm, pencil 4 5/10 cm (4 1/2 cm), chalk 1 4/10 cm

concepts.concept_name: A tenth part: two ways to write a length

content.text:
3.2 A Tenth Part
The length of the pencil shown in the figure below is 3 4/10 units, which can also be read as 3 units and four one-tenths, i.e., (3 × 1) + (4 × 1/10) units.
10 times 1/10 is 1 unit. This length is the same as 34 one-tenths units because 10 one-tenths units make one unit.
34 × 1/10 = 34/10 = 10/10 + 10/10 + 10/10 + 4/10 (34 one-tenths) = 1 + 1 + 1 + 4/10 (3 and 4 one-tenths).
A few numbers with fractional units are shown below along with how to read them. 4 1/10 'four and one-tenth'; 4/10 'four one-tenths' or 'four-tenths'; 41/10 'forty-one one-tenths' or 'forty-one tenths'; 41 1/10 'forty-one and one-tenth'.
For the objects shown below, write their lengths in two ways and read them aloud. An example is given for the USB cable. (Note that the unit length used in each diagram is not the same). The length of the USB cable is 4 and 8/10 units or 48/10 units.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a pencil is 3 units and 4 tenths long. How many tenths is that altogether?
2. One unit is 10 tenths, so 3 units is 30 tenths. Add the 4 tenths and the pencil is 34 tenths long.
3. So every length in tenths can be written in two ways: as whole units and tenths, or as one count of tenths.

content.text:
Worked example: A pencil is 3 4/10 units long. Write its length as a count of tenths and show why it is the same length.
1. 10 one-tenths make 1 unit, so 3 units is 3 × 10 = 30 tenths.
2. 30 tenths and 4 tenths make 34 tenths, so the length is 34/10 units.
3. Check: 34/10 = 10/10 + 10/10 + 10/10 + 4/10, and each 10/10 is 1 unit, so that is 1 + 1 + 1 + 4/10 = 3 4/10.
Answer: 34/10 units
content.publication_text:
Worked example: A pencil is 3 4/10 units long. Write its length as a count of tenths and show why it is the same length.
1. 10 one-tenths make 1 unit, so 3 units is 3 × 10 = 30 tenths.
2. 30 tenths and 4 tenths make 34 tenths, so the length is 34/10 units.
3. Check: 34/10 = 10/10 + 10/10 + 10/10 + 4/10, and each 10/10 is 1 unit, so that is 1 + 1 + 1 + 4/10 = 3 4/10.
Answer: 34/10 units

concepts.concept_name: A tenth part: two ways to write a length

content.text:
Worked example: A USB cable is 4 8/10 units long. Write it in two ways. Then read aloud 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10 and 41 1/10. Three more objects are drawn on their own unit scales: a hand that reaches 1 unit and 6 tenths, a box that is 2 units and 3 tenths, and a leaf that is 3 units and 9 tenths. Write each of these in two ways.
1. USB cable: 4 units and 8 tenths is 4 8/10, and 4 × 10 + 8 = 48 tenths, so 48/10.
2. 4 1/10 is four and one-tenth; 4/10 is four-tenths; 41/10 is forty-one tenths; 41 1/10 is forty-one and one-tenth.
3. Hand: 1 6/10, and 1 × 10 + 6 = 16 tenths, so 16/10.
4. Box: 2 3/10, and 2 × 10 + 3 = 23 tenths, so 23/10.
5. Leaf: 3 9/10, and 3 × 10 + 9 = 39 tenths, so 39/10.
Answer: USB 4 8/10 = 48/10; hand 1 6/10 = 16/10; box 2 3/10 = 23/10; leaf 3 9/10 = 39/10

concepts.concept_name: Ordering lengths written in tenths

content.text:
Worked example: Arrange these lengths in increasing order: 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10 and 41 1/10.
1. As counts of tenths they are 41, 4, 41 and 411.
2. The smallest count is 4, so 4/10 comes first.
3. 41/10 and 4 1/10 are the same length, because both are 41 tenths.
4. The biggest is 41 1/10, which is 411 tenths.
Answer: 4/10, then 4 1/10 and 41/10 (equal), then 41 1/10

A length of units and tenths is also a count of tenths: units times 10, plus the tenths.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How many tenths long is a pencil of three and four tenths?
items: A pencil is 3 4/10 units long. Write its length as a count of tenths and show why it is the same length.
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child has written a length as units and tenths but not yet as a single count of tenths.

interaction_points.prompt: Can we write its length as a count of tenths, and why is it the same length?
covers: A pencil is 3 4/10 units long. Write its length as a count of tenths and show why it is the same length.

source: A pencil is 3 4/10 units long. Write its length as a count of tenths and show why it is the same length.
video_script.why: The child has written a length as units and tenths but not yet as a single count of tenths.
video_script.substitution: Ten tenths make one unit, so three units are thirty tenths, and four more tenths make thirty four tenths.
video_script.anchor: A pencil that is three units and four tenths long, drawn on a bar cut into tenths
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds the 3 units to the 4 tenths to get 3 + 4 = 7 tenths, but 3 units are 30 tenths, so the bubble is struck.

final_answer.spoken: thirty four tenths of a unit

maths_rules: 10 one-tenths make 1 unit, so 3 units = 3 × 10 = 30 tenths.
30 tenths + 4 tenths = 34 tenths, so the length is 34/10 units.
Check: 34 tenths = 10 tenths + 10 tenths + 10 tenths + 4 tenths = 1 + 1 + 1 + 4/10 = 3 4/10.
Slip: 3 + 4 = 7 tenths, but 3 units are 30 tenths.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How can each length be written in two ways?
items: A USB cable is 4 8/10 units long. Write it in two ways. Then read aloud 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10 and 41 1/10. Three more objects are drawn on their own unit scales: a hand that reaches 1 unit and 6 tenths, a box that is 2 units and 3 tenths, and a leaf that is 3 units and 9 tenths. Write each of these in two ways.

interaction_points.prompt: How can we write this length in two ways, and how do we read such numbers aloud?
covers: A USB cable is 4 8/10 units long. Write it in two ways. Then read aloud 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10 and 41 1/10. Three more objects are drawn on their own unit scales: a hand that reaches 1 unit and 6 tenths, a box that is 2 units and 3 tenths, and a leaf that is 3 units and 9 tenths. Write each of these in two ways.

source: A USB cable is 4 8/10 units long. Write it in two ways. Then read aloud 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10 and 41 1/10. Three more objects are drawn on their own unit scales: a hand that reaches 1 unit and 6 tenths, a box that is 2 units and 3 tenths, and a leaf that is 3 units and 9 tenths. Write each of these in two ways.
video_script.why: The child can turn units and tenths into one count of tenths for one length and now does it for four lengths and reads such numbers aloud.
video_script.substitution: Multiply the units by ten and add the tenths to get the count of tenths.

final_answer.spoken: the cable is forty eight tenths, the hand is sixteen tenths, the box is twenty three tenths, and the leaf is thirty nine tenths

concepts.concept_name: Adding lengths in tenths

content.text:
Sonu is measuring some of his body parts. The length of Sonu's lower arm is 2 7/10 units, and that of his upper arm is 3 6/10 units. What is the total length of his arm?
To get the total length, let us see the lower and upper arm length as 2 units and 7 one-tenths, and 3 units and 6 one-tenths, respectively. So, there are (2 + 3) units and (7 + 6) one-tenths. Together, they make 5 units and 13 one-tenths. But 13 one-tenths is 1 unit and 3 one-tenths. So, the total length is 6 units and 3 one-tenths.
(2 + 3) + (7/10 + 6/10) = (2 + 3) + (13/10) = 5 + 13/10 = 5 + 10/10 + 3/10 = 5 + 1 + 3/10 = 6 + 3/10 = 6 3/10.
Or, both the lengths can be converted to tenths and then added: 27 one-tenths and 36 one-tenths is 63 one-tenths, 27/10 + 36/10 = 63/10. 63/10 is the same as 60 one-tenths (60/10) and 3 one-tenths (3/10), which is equal to 6 units and 3 one-tenths, i.e., 6 3/10.
The lengths of the body parts of a honeybee are given. Find its total length. Head: 2 3/10 units. Thorax: 5 4/10 units. Abdomen: 7 5/10 units.

content.text:
Worked example: Sonu's lower arm is 2 7/10 units and his upper arm is 3 6/10 units. What is the total length of his arm? Add in the two ways.
1. Units: 2 + 3 = 5. Tenths: 7/10 + 6/10 = 13/10.
2. 13 tenths is 1 unit and 3 tenths, so 5 + 13/10 = 5 + 10/10 + 3/10 = 5 + 1 + 3/10 = 6 3/10.
3. In tenths: 2 7/10 is 27/10 and 3 6/10 is 36/10, and 27/10 + 36/10 = 63/10.
4. 63/10 is 60/10 + 3/10, which is 6 units and 3 tenths, so 6 3/10 again.
Answer: 6 3/10 units

content.text:
Worked example: The parts of a honeybee are 2 3/10 units (head), 5 4/10 units (thorax) and 7 5/10 units (abdomen). Find its total length.
1. Whole units: 2 + 5 + 7 = 14.
2. Tenths: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 tenths, which is 1 unit and 2 tenths.
3. Total: 14 + 1 = 15 units and 2 tenths.
Answer: 15 2/10 units

concepts.concept_name: Subtracting lengths in tenths

content.text:
The length of Shylaja's hand is 12 4/10 units, and her palm is 6 7/10 units, as shown in the picture. What is the length of the longest (middle) finger?
The length of the finger can be found by evaluating (12 + 4/10) − (6 + 7/10). This can be done in different ways. For example, (a) 12 + 4/10 − 6 − 7/10 = (12 − 6) + (4/10 − 7/10) = 6 − 3/10 = 5 + 1 − 3/10 = 5 + 10/10 − 3/10 = 5 + 7/10 = 5 7/10. Discuss what is being done here and why.
(b) As in the case of counting numbers, it is convenient to start subtraction from the tenths. We cannot remove 7 one-tenths from 4 one-tenths. So we split a unit from 12 and convert it to 10 one-tenths. Now, the number has 11 units and 14 one-tenths. We subtract 7 one-tenths from 14 one-tenths and then subtract 6 units from 11 units. 12 4/10 becomes 11 14/10, and 11 14/10 − 6 7/10 = 5 7/10.
Try computing the difference by converting both lengths to tenths.

content.text:
Worked example: Shylaja's hand is 12 4/10 units long and her palm is 6 7/10 units. How long is her middle finger? Solve it by breaking a unit, and check by converting to tenths.
1. There are only 4 tenths in the hand, and 7 tenths must be taken away.
2. Break 1 unit of the 12 into 10 tenths: 12 4/10 becomes 11 14/10.
3. 14 tenths − 7 tenths = 7 tenths, and 11 units − 6 units = 5 units, so 5 7/10.
4. Check in tenths: 124/10 − 67/10 = 57/10 = 5 7/10.
Answer: 5 7/10 units

concepts.concept_name: Subtracting lengths in tenths

content.text:
Worked example: A Celestial Pearl Danio is 2 4/10 cm long and a Philippine Goby is 9/10 cm long. What is the difference in their lengths?
1. Write both in tenths: 2 4/10 is 24/10, and the goby is 9/10.
2. 24/10 − 9/10 = 15/10.
3. 15 tenths is 1 unit and 5 tenths, so the difference is 1 5/10 cm.
4. Compare with your finger, which is about 6 to 8 cm long: the Danio is about 2 1/2 cm and the Goby less than 1 cm, so both fish are much shorter than a finger.
Answer: 1 5/10 cm

source_video_walkthrough.title: How long is the middle finger of Ziva?

source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child has added lengths with units and tenths and now takes one length away from another when the tenths are too few.

interaction_points.prompt: How long is it?
covers: The hand is 12 4/10 units long and the palm is 6 7/10 units. How long is the middle finger? Solve it by breaking a unit, and check by converting to tenths.

source: The hand is 12 4/10 units long and the palm is 6 7/10 units. How long is the middle finger? Solve it by breaking a unit, and check by converting to tenths.
video_script.why: The child has added lengths with units and tenths and now takes one length away from another when the tenths are too few.
video_script.substitution: When the tenths are too few, break one unit into ten tenths, then take away units and tenths separately.
video_script.anchor: A hand with its palm marked from the wrist and the middle finger as the rest, drawn along a unit scale
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko takes the smaller tenths number from the bigger one, 7 - 4 = 3, and 12 - 6 = 6, to get 6 3/10, but the 4 tenths of the hand cannot give up 7 tenths, so a unit must be broken.

maths_rules: Break 1 unit of the 12 into 10 tenths: 12 4/10 = 11 + 10/10 + 4/10 = 11 14/10.

video_script.why: The child can add and subtract numbers with tenths and now uses the difference of two neighbours to continue six patterns.

concepts.concept_name: Splitting a tenth into ten parts

content.text:
3.3 A Hundredth Part
The length of a sheet of paper was 8 9/10 units, which can also be said as 8 units and 9 one-tenths. It is folded in half along its length. What is its length now?
We can say that its length is between 4 4/10 units and 4 5/10 units. But we cannot state its exact measurement, since there are no markings. Earlier, we split a unit into 10 one-tenths to measure smaller lengths. We can do something similar and split each one-tenth into 10 parts.
What is the length of this smaller part? How many such smaller parts make a unit length?
As shown in the figure below, each one-tenth has 10 smaller parts, and there are 10 one-tenths in a unit; therefore, there will be 100 smaller parts in a unit. Therefore, one part's length will be 1/100 of a unit.
Returning to our question, what is the length of the folded paper? We can see that it ends at 4 4/10 5/100, read as 4 units and 4 one-tenths and 5 one-hundredths.
Math Talk: How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can we also say that the length is 4 units and 45 one-hundredths?

content.text:
1. Predict first: half of 8 9/10 is more than 4 4/10 but less than 4 5/10. Which mark can name it?
2. No mark does, so each tenth is split again into 10 equal parts. There are 10 tenths in a unit, so there are 10 × 10 = 100 small parts in a unit.
3. Each small part is 1/100 of a unit, called one-hundredth. 10 hundredths make 1 tenth.

content.text:
Worked example: A paper strip 8 9/10 units long is folded in half. Its new length ends between 4 4/10 and 4 5/10. Split each tenth into 10 parts: what is one small part, and where does the folded strip end? Can the length also be said as 4 units and 45 hundredths?
1. Each tenth has 10 smaller parts and a unit has 10 tenths, so a unit has 10 × 10 = 100 smaller parts.
2. One part is 1/100 of a unit.
3. The folded strip ends 5 parts after the 4 4/10 mark, so it is 4 units and 4 tenths and 5 hundredths.
4. 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so 4 tenths is 40 hundredths, and 40 + 5 = 45 hundredths.
5. So yes, the length is also 4 units and 45 hundredths, that is 4 45/100.
Answer: 4 4/10 5/100, which is also 4 45/100 units

concepts.concept_name: Reading lengths in hundredths

content.text:
Worked example: Marks on a wire, measured from 0, are 1 part, 2 tenths, 20 parts, 55 parts, 99 parts, 130 parts, 155 parts, 174 parts, 202 parts and 240 parts from 0, where each part is one hundredth. Write each length as a fraction of a unit.
1. 1 part is 1/100.
2. 2 tenths is 2/10, which is 20/100, the same as the mark 20 parts.
3. 55 parts is 55/100 and 99 parts is 99/100.
4. 130 parts is 130/100, which is 1 30/100 or 1 3/10.
5. 155 parts is 155/100, which is 1 55/100.
6. 174 parts is 174/100, which is 1 74/100.
7. 202 parts is 202/100, which is 2 2/100.
8. 240 parts is 240/100, which is 2 40/100 or 2 4/10.
Answer: 1/100, 2/10, 20/100, 55/100, 99/100, 130/100, 155/100, 174/100, 202/100, 240/100

source_video_walkthrough.title: Where does the folded paper strip end?
items: A paper strip 8 9/10 units long is folded in half. Its new length ends between 4 4/10 and 4 5/10. Split each tenth into 10 parts: what is one small part, and where does the folded strip end? Can the length also be said as 4 units and 45 hundredths?
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child can name tenths but meets a length that falls between two tenth marks, so a smaller part is needed.

interaction_points.prompt: Where does the folded strip end, and what is the small part there?
covers: A paper strip 8 9/10 units long is folded in half. Its new length ends between 4 4/10 and 4 5/10. Split each tenth into 10 parts: what is one small part, and where does the folded strip end? Can the length also be said as 4 units and 45 hundredths?

source: A paper strip 8 9/10 units long is folded in half. Its new length ends between 4 4/10 and 4 5/10. Split each tenth into 10 parts: what is one small part, and where does the folded strip end? Can the length also be said as 4 units and 45 hundredths?
video_script.why: The child can name tenths but meets a length that falls between two tenth marks, so a smaller part is needed.
video_script.substitution: Split each tenth into ten parts, so a unit has one hundred parts and one part is a hundredth.
video_script.anchor: A paper strip folded in half, with its end between the 4 4/10 mark and the 4 5/10 mark of a unit scale
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko calls the small part one tenth because it lies inside a tenth, but a tenth is cut into 10 parts, so one part is only 1/100 of a unit.
video_script.payoff_line: The folded strip is four units and forty five hundredths long

final_answer.spoken: four units, four tenths and five hundredths, which is also four units and forty five hundredths

maths_rules: Each tenth is split into 10 parts; a unit has 10 tenths, so 10 × 10 = 100 parts.
One part is 1/100 of a unit, a hundredth.
The strip ends 5 parts after the 4 4/10 mark, so it is 4 units, 4 tenths and 5 hundredths.
10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so 4 tenths = 40 hundredths and 40 + 5 = 45 hundredths.
Slip: the small part is not 1/10, it is 1/100.
video_script.design: One idea: a unit split into tenths and each tenth into ten parts has one hundred parts, and one part is a hundredth. Assumes the child knows tenths. Wrong idea: the small part is a tenth. The strip and its scale stay all video; the zoomed gap builds in the ground part.

items: Marks on a wire, measured from 0, are 1 part, 2 tenths, 20 parts, 55 parts, 99 parts, 130 parts, 155 parts, 174 parts, 202 parts and 240 parts from 0, where each part is one hundredth. Write each length as a fraction of a unit.

interaction_points.prompt: Can we write every mark as a fraction of a unit?
covers: Marks on a wire, measured from 0, are 1 part, 2 tenths, 20 parts, 55 parts, 99 parts, 130 parts, 155 parts, 174 parts, 202 parts and 240 parts from 0, where each part is one hundredth. Write each length as a fraction of a unit.

source: Marks on a wire, measured from 0, are 1 part, 2 tenths, 20 parts, 55 parts, 99 parts, 130 parts, 155 parts, 174 parts, 202 parts and 240 parts from 0, where each part is one hundredth. Write each length as a fraction of a unit.
video_script.why: The child can write one length in three ways and now writes ten marks on a wire as fractions of a unit.
video_script.substitution: A mark that is some number of parts from zero is that many hundredths of a unit.
video_script.anchor: A wire from zero with ten marks, each labelled by how many parts from zero, and one labelled in tenths
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko reads 2 tenths as 2/100 because both have the number 2, but a tenth is 10 hundredths, so 2 tenths is 20 hundredths.
video_script.payoff_line: Each mark is its number of parts over one hundred

final_answer.spoken: each mark is its number of parts over one hundred, and two tenths is the same as twenty hundredths

maths_rules: One part is 1/100 of a unit.
2 tenths = 2/10 = 20/100, the same place as the mark 20 parts.
100 parts make 1 unit, so a count over 100 gives a fraction bigger than 1.
Slip: 2 tenths is not 2/100, it is 20/100.
video_script.design: One idea: a mark counted in parts is that many hundredths of a unit. Assumes the child knows that a unit has one hundred parts. Wrong idea: read two tenths as two hundredths. The wire stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part. The list of marks is on the board and is not all spoken.

concepts.concept_name: Adding with tenths and hundredths

content.text:
What will be the sum of 15 3/10 4/100 and 2 6/10 8/100? This can be solved in different ways. Some are shown below.
Method 1: (15 + 2) + (3/10 + 6/10) + (4/100 + 8/100) = 17 + 9/10 + 12/100 = 17 + 9/10 + 1/10 + 2/100 = 17 + 10/10 + 2/100 = 18 2/100. 10 hundredths is the same as 1 tenth.
Method 2: written as a column, the tenths add to 9 and the hundredths add to 12, which is 1 tenth and 2 hundredths, so 10 tenths, which is 1 unit, and 2 hundredths: 18 2/100.
Math Talk: Are both these methods different? Observe the addition done below for 483 + 268. Do you see any similarities between the methods shown above? (400 + 80 + 3) + (200 + 60 + 8) = (400 + 200) + (80 + 60) + (3 + 8) = 600 + 140 + 11 = 600 + 150 + 1 = 700 + 50 + 1 = 751.
One can also find the sum 15 3/10 4/100 + 2 6/10 8/100 by converting to hundredths, as follows. (c) (15 + 2) + (34/100 + 68/100) = 17 + 102/100 = 17 + 1 + 2/100 = 18 2/100. (d) 1534/100 + 268/100 = 1802/100 = 1800/100 + 2/100 = 18 2/100.
100 hundredths is same as 1 unit. 15 is the same as 1500 hundredths and 2 is the same as 200 hundredths.

1. Predict first: 15 3/10 4/100 plus 2 6/10 8/100. Will the hundredths together reach 10?
2. Add hundredths to hundredths, tenths to tenths and units to units. When 10 hundredths appear, regroup them as 1 tenth.
3. This is the same carrying we do for 483 + 268, with places worth 10 times each other.
4. Or convert both to hundredths, add the counts, and write the result back in units.

content.text:
Worked example: Add 15 3/10 4/100 and 2 6/10 8/100 by adding place by place, and compare with the addition 483 + 268.
1. Units: 15 + 2 = 17. Tenths: 3 + 6 = 9. Hundredths: 4 + 8 = 12.
2. 12 hundredths is 1 tenth and 2 hundredths, so the tenths become 9 + 1 = 10 tenths.
3. 10 tenths is 1 unit, so the units become 17 + 1 = 18, leaving 2 hundredths: 18 2/100.
4. In 483 + 268 the ones add to 11, so one ten is carried; the tens add to 150, so one hundred is carried. It is the same carrying, with a different set of places.
Answer: 18 2/100

concepts.concept_name: Subtracting with tenths and hundredths

content.text:
What is the difference: 25 9/10 − 6 4/10 7/100? One way to solve this is as follows: there are not enough hundredths, so 25 9/10 is written as 25 8/10 10/100, and then 25 8/10 10/100 − 6 4/10 7/100 = 19 4/10 3/100.
Math Talk: Solve this by converting to hundredths.
What is the difference 15 3/10 4/100 − 2 6/10 8/100? One way to solve this is as follows: 15 3/10 4/100 becomes 15 2/10 14/100 and then 14 12/10 14/100, and 14 12/10 14/100 − 2 6/10 8/100 = 12 6/10 6/100.
Math Talk: Observe the subtraction done below for 653 − 268. Do you see any similarities with the methods shown above? (600 + 50 + 3) − (200 + 60 + 8) = (600 − 200) + (50 − 60) + (3 − 8) = (600 − 200) + (40 − 60) + (13 − 8) = (600 − 200) + (40 − 60) + 5 = (500 − 200) + (140 − 60) + 5 = 300 + 80 + 5 = 385.

concepts.concept_name: Subtracting with tenths and hundredths

content.text:
Worked example: Find 15 3/10 4/100 − 2 6/10 8/100, and compare the steps with 653 − 268.
1. Hundredths: 4 is less than 8, so break 1 tenth: 15 3/10 4/100 becomes 15 2/10 14/100.
2. Tenths: 2 is less than 6, so break 1 unit into 10 tenths: 15 2/10 14/100 becomes 14 12/10 14/100.
3. Hundredths: 14 − 8 = 6. Tenths: 12 − 6 = 6. Units: 14 − 2 = 12. So the answer is 12 6/10 6/100.
4. In 653 − 268 the ones are too few, so a ten is broken into ones, and then a hundred into tens. It is the same breaking down, one place at a time.
Answer: 12 6/10 6/100

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (hundredths), the set of six sums and differences

content.text:
Figure it Out (hundredths), the set of six sums and differences: Find the sums and differences: (a) 3/10 + 3 4/100 (b) 9 5/10 7/100 + 2 1/10 3/100 (c) 15 6/10 4/100 + 14 3/10 6/100 (d) 7 7/100 − 4 4/100 (e) 8 6/100 − 5 3/100 (f) 12 6/10 2/100 − 9/10 9/100
1. (a) 3/10 is 30/100, so 30/100 + 3 4/100 = 3 34/100.
2. (b) Units: 9 + 2 = 11. Tenths: 5 + 1 = 6. Hundredths: 7 + 3 = 10, which is 1 tenth, so the tenths are 7: 11 7/10.
3. (c) Units: 15 + 14 = 29. Tenths: 6 + 3 = 9. Hundredths: 4 + 6 = 10, which carries 1 tenth, so the tenths are 10, which carries 1 unit: 30.
4. (d) Hundredths: 7 − 4 = 3. Tenths: 0. Units: 7 − 4 = 3. So 3 3/100.
5. (e) Hundredths: 6 − 3 = 3. Units: 8 − 5 = 3. So 3 3/100.
6. (f) 12 6/10 2/100 has 2 hundredths, and 9 must be taken away: break 1 tenth to get 12 5/10 12/100. Hundredths: 12 − 9 = 3. Tenths: 5 is less than 9, so break 1 unit: 11 15/10 12/100, 15 − 9 = 6. Units: 11 − 0 = 11. So 11 6/10 3/100, which is 11 63/100.
Answer: (a) 3 34/100 (b) 11 7/10 (c) 30 (d) 3 3/100 (e) 3 3/100 (f) 11 63/100

concepts.concept_name: Why split a unit into ten parts

content.text:
3.4 Decimal Place Value
You may have noticed that whenever we need to measure something more accurately, we split a part into 10 (smaller) equal parts ― we split a unit into 10 one-tenths and then split each one-tenth into 10, one-hundredths and then we use these smaller parts to measure.
Can we not split a unit into 4 equal parts, 5 equal parts, 8 equal parts, or any other number of equal parts instead?
Yes, we can. The example below compares how the same length is represented when the unit is split into 10 equal parts and when the unit is split into 4 equal parts.
If an even more precise measure is needed, each quarter can further be split into four equal parts. Each part then measures 1/16 of a unit, i.e., 16 such parts make 1 unit.
Then why split a unit into 10 parts every time?
The reason is the special role that 10 plays in the Indian place value system. For a whole number written in the Indian place value system ― for example, 281 ― the place value of 2 is hundreds (100), that of 8 is tens (10), and that of 1 is one (1). Each place value is 10 times bigger than the one immediately to its right. Equivalently, each place value is 10 times smaller than the one immediately to its left: 10 ones make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred, 10 hundreds make 1 thousand, and so on.

content.text:
Worked example: A unit is split into 4 equal parts, and each part is split into 4 equal parts again. How many tiny parts make a unit, and how is that different from splitting by 10 twice?
1. First split: 4 equal parts, each 1/4 of a unit.
2. Second split: each quarter into 4 parts, so 4 × 4 = 16 parts in a unit, each 1/16 of a unit.
3. Splitting by 10 twice gives 10 × 10 = 100 parts, each 1/100 of a unit.
4. In the number 281 each place is 10 times the place on its right: 10 ones make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred. Splitting a unit into 10 keeps that same rule going to the right of the ones.
Answer: 16 parts of 1/16 each, against 100 parts of 1/100 each; 10 matches the 10 times rule of the places

concepts.concept_name: Tenths, hundredths, thousandths and the decimal system

content.text:
In order to extend this system of writing numbers to quantities smaller than one, we divide one into 10 equal parts. What does this give? It gives one-tenth. Further dividing it into 10 parts gives one-hundredth, and so on.
Can we extend this further? What will the fraction be when 1/100 is split into 10 equal parts?
It will be 1/1000, i.e., a thousand such parts make up a unit.
Just as when we extend to the left of 10,000, we get bigger place values at each step, we can also extend to the right of 1/1000, getting smaller place values at each step.
This way of writing numbers is called the “decimal system” since it is based on the number 10; “decem” means ten in Latin, which in turn is cognate to the Sanskrit daśha meaning 10, with similar words for 10 occurring across many Indian languages including Odia, Konkani, Marathi, Gujarati, Hindi, Kashmiri, Bodo, and Assamese. We shall learn about other ways of writing numbers in later grades.

content.text:
1. Predict first: split one hundredth into 10 equal parts. What fraction of a unit is each part?
2. 100 × 10 = 1000, so each part is 1/1000 of a unit, called a thousandth.
3. The ladder now runs 1000, 100, 10, 1, then 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000 and on. Each step right divides by 10 and each step left multiplies by 10.
4. A system built on ten is called decimal, from the word for ten.

content.text:
Worked example: Split one hundredth into 10 equal parts. What is one part called, and how many make a unit? Then write the ladder of place values from 1000 down to a thousandth.
1. One unit has 100 hundredths, and each hundredth is split into 10 parts.
2. So a unit has 100 × 10 = 1000 parts, and each part is 1/1000 of a unit, one thousandth.
3. The ladder is 1000, 100, 10, 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000.
4. Going one step to the right divides by 10; going one step to the left multiplies by 10.
Answer: 1/1000 of a unit, one thousandth; 1000 of them make a unit

So a unit has 100 × 10 = 1000 parts, and each part is 1/1000 of a unit, one thousandth.
Going one step to the right divides by 10; going one step to the left multiplies by 10.
content.answer: 1/1000 of a unit, one thousandth; 1000 of them make a unit

concepts.concept_name: How big? Counting parts of different places

content.text:
How Big?
We already know that a hundred 10s make 1000, and a hundred 100s make 10000.
We can ask similar questions about fractional parts: (a) How many thousandths make one unit? (b) How many thousandths make one tenth? (c) How many thousandths make one hundredth? (d) How many tenths make one ten? (e) How many hundredths make one ten?
Make a few more questions of this kind and answer them.

content.text:
Worked example: (a) How many thousandths make one unit? (b) How many make one tenth? (c) How many make one hundredth? (d) How many tenths make one ten? (e) How many hundredths make one ten?
1. (a) From a unit to a thousandth is 3 steps of 10, so 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 thousandths.
2. (b) From a tenth to a thousandth is 2 steps, so 100 thousandths.
3. (c) From a hundredth to a thousandth is 1 step, so 10 thousandths.
4. (d) A ten is 10 units and each unit is 10 tenths, so 100 tenths.
5. (e) A ten is 100 tenths and each tenth is 10 hundredths, so 1000 hundredths.
6. Own question: how many hundredths make one tenth? One step, so 10.
Answer: (a) 1000 (b) 100 (c) 10 (d) 100 (e) 1000

concepts.concept_name: Practice: how many of one place make one of another

content.text:
Each step right on the ladder divides by 10, and each step left multiplies by 10.
Count the steps between two places, and multiply 10 for each step.
Ten hundredths make a tenth, and a thousand thousandths make a unit.

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q13: Which is greater? (a) 10/1000 or 1/10 (b) one-hundredth or 90 thousandths (c) one-thousandth or 90 hundredths
1. (a) 10/1000 is 10 thousandths. A tenth is 100 thousandths. 100 is more than 10, so 1/10 is greater.
2. (b) One hundredth is 10 thousandths. 90 thousandths is more than 10 thousandths, so 90 thousandths is greater.
3. (c) 90 hundredths is 900 thousandths, far more than 1 thousandth, so 90 hundredths is greater.
Answer: (a) 1/10 is greater (b) 90 thousandths is greater (c) 90 hundredths is greater

concepts.concept_name: Why we need a point

content.text:
Notation, Writing and Reading of Numbers
We have been writing numbers in a particular way, say 456, instead of writing them as 4 × 100 (4 hundreds) + 5 × 10 (5 tens) + 6 × 1 (6 ones). Similarly, can we skip writing tenths and hundredths?
Can the quantity 4 2/10 be written as 42 (skipping the 1/10 in 2 × 1/10)? If yes, how would we know if 42 means 4 tens and 2 units or it means 4 units and 2 tenths?
Similarly, 705 could mean: (a) 7 hundreds, and 0 tens and 5 ones (700 + 0 + 5) (b) 7 tens and 0 units and 5 tenths (70 + 0 + 5/10) (c) 7 units and 0 tenths and 5 hundredths (7 + 0/10 + 5/100)
Since these are different quantities, we need to have distinct ways of writing them.
To identify the place value where integers end and the fractional parts start, we use a point or period (‘.’) as a separator, called a decimal point.
The above quantities in decimal notation are then: 7 hundreds and 5 ones is 705; 7 tens and 5 tenths is 70.5; 7 units and 5 hundredths is 7.05.
Thus decimal notation is a natural extension of the Indian place value system to numbers also having fractional parts. Just as 705 means 7 × 100 + 5 × 1, the number 70.5 means 7 × 10 + 5 × 1/10, and 7.05 means 7 × 1 + 5 × 1/100.

content.text:
Worked example: The digits 7, 0 and 5 can mean 7 hundreds and 5 ones, or 7 tens and 5 tenths, or 7 units and 5 hundredths. Write each quantity in decimal notation and show the place of each digit.
1. 7 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones is 700 + 0 + 5 = 705: no point is needed.
2. 7 tens, 0 units, 5 tenths is 70 + 0 + 5/10, written 70.5: the 7 is tens, the 0 is units, the 5 is tenths.
3. 7 units, 0 tenths, 5 hundredths is 7 + 0/10 + 5/100, written 7.05: the 7 is units, the 0 is tenths, the 5 is hundredths.
4. So 705, 70.5 and 7.05 are three different quantities, and the point shows which is which.
Answer: 705, 70.5 and 7.05

concepts.concept_name: Reading decimals and the place table

content.text:
We have seen how to write numbers using the decimal point (‘.’). But how do we read/say these numbers?
We know that 705 is read as seven hundred and five. 70.5 is read as seventy point five, short for seventy and five-tenths. 7.05 is read as seven point zero five, short for seven and five hundredths.
0.274 is read as zero point two seven four. We don’t read it as zero point two hundred and seventy four as 0.274 means 2 one-tenths and 7 one-hundredths and 4 one-thousandths.

concepts.concept_name: Counts of tenths and hundredths as decimals

content.text:
In the chapter on large numbers, we learned how to write 23 hundreds.
23 hundreds = 23 × 100 = 2000 + 300 = 2300.
Similarly, 23 tens would be: 23 tens = 23 × 10 = 200 + 30 = 230.
How can we write 234 tenths in decimal form? 234 tenths = 234/10 = 200/10 + 30/10 + 4/10 = 20 + 3 + 4/10 = 23.4.
Write these quantities in decimal form: (a) 234 hundredths, (b) 105 tenths.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students show that 705 can mean three different quantities if the places are not marked, and explain how a decimal point separates the whole part from the fractional part.
Students read a decimal digit by digit after the point, and write quantities given in places in decimal form with a place value table.
Students write a count of hundreds, tens, tenths or hundredths as a decimal by splitting it into places or by moving the point.
Students write fractions and quantities as decimals, split decimals into tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and read them aloud.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q1: Convert the following fractions into decimals: (a) 5/100 (b) 16/1000 (c) 12/10 (d) 254/1000
1. (a) 5/100 is 5 hundredths, so the 5 sits in the hundredths place: 0.05.
2. (b) 16/1000 is 1 hundredth and 6 thousandths, so 0.016.
3. (c) 12/10 is 1 unit and 2 tenths, so 1.2.
4. (d) 254/1000 is 2 tenths, 5 hundredths and 4 thousandths, so 0.254.
Answer: (a) 0.05 (b) 0.016 (c) 1.2 (d) 0.254

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q2: Convert the following decimals into a sum of tenths, hundredths and thousandths: (a) 0.34 (b) 1.02 (c) 0.8 (d) 0.362
1. (a) 0.34 has 3 tenths and 4 hundredths: 3/10 + 4/100.
2. (b) 1.02 has 1 unit, 0 tenths and 2 hundredths: 1 + 2/100, where the unit is 100/100.
3. (c) 0.8 has 8 tenths: 8/10.
4. (d) 0.362 has 3 tenths, 6 hundredths and 2 thousandths: 3/10 + 6/100 + 2/1000.
Answer: (a) 3/10 + 4/100 (b) 100/100 + 2/100, which is 1 + 2/100 (c) 8/10 (d) 3/10 + 6/100 + 2/1000

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q14

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q14: Write the decimal forms of the quantities mentioned. An example is given: 87 ones, 5 tenths and 60 hundredths is 88.10. (a) 12 tens and 12 tenths (b) 10 tens, 10 ones, 10 tenths, and 10 hundredths (c) 25 tens, 25 ones, 25 tenths, and 25 hundredths
1. Example: 87 + 0.5 + 0.60 = 88.10, since 60 hundredths is 6 tenths.
2. (a) 12 tens is 120, and 12 tenths is 1.2, so 121.2.
3. (b) 10 tens is 100, 10 ones is 10, 10 tenths is 1, and 10 hundredths is 0.1, so 111.1.
4. (c) 25 tens is 250, 25 ones is 25, 25 tenths is 2.5, and 25 hundredths is 0.25: 250 + 25 + 2.5 + 0.25 = 277.75.
Answer: (a) 121.2 (b) 111.1 (c) 277.75

concepts.concept_name: Length: millimetres, centimetres and metres

content.text:
3.5 Units of Measurement
Length Conversion
We have been using a scale to measure length for a few years. We already know that 1 cm = 10 mm (millimeters). How many cm is 1 mm?
1 mm = 1/10 cm = 0.1 cm (i.e., one-tenth of a cm). How many cm is (a) 5 mm? (b) 12 mm?
5 mm = 5/10 cm = 0.5 cm. 12 mm = 10 mm + 2 mm = 1 cm + 2/10 cm = 1.2 cm.
How many mm is 5.6 cm? Since each cm has 10 mm, 5.6 cm (5 cm + 0.6 cm) is 56 mm.
Fill in the blanks below (mm to cm): 12 mm = 1.2 cm, 56 mm = 5.6 cm, 70 mm = _____, _____ = 0.9 cm, 134 mm = _____, _____ = 203.6 cm
We also know that 1 m = 100 cm. Based on this, we can say that 1 cm = 1/100 m = 0.01 m.
How many m is (a) 10 cm? (b) 15 cm? 10 cm = 10/100 m = 1/10 m = 0.1 m. Since each cm is one-hundredth of a meter, 15 cm can be written as 15 cm = 15/100 m = 10/100 m + 5/100 m = 1/10 m + 5/100 m = 0.15 m.
Fill in the blanks below (cm to m): 36 cm = _____, 50 cm = _____, _____ = 0.89 m, 4 cm = _____, 325 cm = _____, _____ = 2.07 m
How many mm does 1 meter have? Can we write 1 mm = 1/1000 m?

Worked example: Fill in the blanks (cm to m): 36 cm, 50 cm, the cm that make 0.89 m, 4 cm, 325 cm, and the cm that make 2.07 m. How many mm make 1 m, and can we write 1 mm = 1/1000 m?
1. 1 cm is 1/100 m = 0.01 m. 36 cm = 0.36 m. 50 cm = 0.50 m = 0.5 m.
2. 0.89 m = 89 cm. 4 cm = 0.04 m. 325 cm = 3.25 m. 2.07 m = 207 cm.
3. 1 m = 100 cm and each cm is 10 mm, so 100 × 10 = 1000 mm make 1 m.
4. So 1 mm is 1/1000 of a metre, and yes, we can write 1 mm = 1/1000 m = 0.001 m.

concepts.concept_name: Weight: grams, kilograms and milligrams

content.text:
Weight Conversion
Let us look at kilograms (kg). We know that 1 kg = 1000 gram (g). We can say that 1 g = 1/1000 kg = 0.001 kg.
How many kilograms is 5 g? 5 g = 5/1000 kg = 0.005 kg. How many kilograms is 10 g? 10 g = 10/1000 kg = 1/100 kg = 0.010 kg.
As each gram is one-thousandth of a kg, 254 g can be written as 254 g = 254/1000 kg = (200/1000 + 50/1000 + 4/1000) kg = (2/10 + 5/100 + 4/1000) kg = 0.254 kg.
Fill in the blanks below (g to kg): 465 g = _____, 68 g = _____, 1560 g = _____, 704 g = _____, _____ = 0.56 kg, _____ = 2.5 kg
Look at the picture below showing different quantities of rice. Starting from the 1g heap, subsequent heaps can be found that are 10 times heavier than the previous heap/packets. The combined weight of rice in this picture is 11.111 kg.
Also, 1 gram = 1000 milligrams (mg). So, 1 mg = 1/1000 g = 0.001 g.

concepts.concept_name: Money: paise and rupees

content.text:
Rupee ─ Paise conversion
You may have heard of ‘paisa’. 100 paise is equal to 1 rupee. As we have coins and notes for rupees, coins for paise were also used commonly until recently. There were coins for 1 paisa, 2 paise, 3 paise, 5 paise, 10 paise, 20 paise, 25 paise, and 50 paise. All denominations of 25 paise and less were removed from use in the year 2011. But we still see paise in bills, account statements, etc.
1 rupee = 100 paise. 1 paisa = 1/100 rupee = 0.01 rupee. As each paisa is one-hundredth of a rupee, 75 paise = 75/100 rupee = (70/100 + 5/100) rupee = (7/10 + 5/100) rupee = 0.75 rupee.
Fill in the blanks below (rupee to paise): 10 p = _____, _____ p = ₹ 0.05, _____ p = ₹ 0.36, _____ = ₹ 0.50, 99 p = _____, 250 p = _____
During the 1970s, a masala dosa cost just 50 paise, one could buy a banana for 20 to 25 paise, a handful of peppermints were available for 2 paise or 3 paise, and a kg of rice cost ₹2.45.
Discuss with adults at home/school the prices of different products and services during their childhood. Try to find old coins and stamps.

content.text:
Worked example: Fill in the blanks (paise to rupees): 10 p, 5 p, 36 p, 50 p, 99 p, 250 p. Then write 75 paise in rupees, step by step.
1. 1 paisa is 1/100 rupee = ₹0.01, so the point moves 2 places left.
2. 75 paise = 75/100 rupee = 70/100 + 5/100 = 7/10 + 5/100 = ₹0.75.
3. 10 p = ₹0.10. 5 p = ₹0.05. 36 p = ₹0.36. 50 p = ₹0.50. 99 p = ₹0.99. 250 p = ₹2.50.

concepts.concept_name: Money: paise and rupees

content.text:
Worked example: A masala dosa cost 50 paise in the 1970s, and a kg of rice cost ₹2.45. Write the dosa price in rupees, and say how many such dosas the rice price would buy.
1. 50 paise = ₹0.50.
2. A kg of rice cost ₹2.45, which is 245 paise.
3. 245 ÷ 50 = 4.9, so the rice price would buy 4 dosas and a little more.
4. Prices from your own elders' childhood can be written the same way in rupees with a decimal.
Answer: ₹0.50 for the dosa; ₹2.45 buys 4 dosas with 45 paise left

concepts.concept_name: Practice: convert between units

content.text:
Find the exchange rate between the two units: 10, 100 or 1000.
To a bigger unit, divide, which moves the point left; to a smaller unit, multiply, which moves it right.
Check by converting back.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students convert between millimetres and centimetres and between centimetres and metres by using one tenth and one hundredth as the exchange rates.
Students convert between grams and kilograms with one thousandth as the exchange rate, and between milligrams and grams.
Students convert between paise and rupees with one hundredth as the exchange rate, and compare old and new prices.
Students convert lengths, weights and money between a bigger and a smaller unit by moving the decimal point.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q11

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q11: How many millimetres make 1 kilometre?
1. 1 km = 1000 m.
2. 1 m = 1000 mm.
3. So 1 km = 1000 × 1000 mm = 1000000 mm.
Answer: 1000000 mm (ten lakh millimetres)

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q12

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q12: Indian Railways offers optional travel insurance for passengers who book e-tickets. It costs 45 paise per passenger. If 1 lakh people opt for insurance in a day, what is the total insurance fee paid?
1. 1 lakh is 100000 passengers.
2. Total in paise: 45 × 100000 = 4500000 paise.
3. 100 paise make 1 rupee, so 4500000 paise = ₹45000.
Answer: ₹45,000

concepts.concept_name: Tenths and hundredths on the number line

content.text:
3.6 Locating and Comparing Decimals
Let us consider the decimal number 1.4. It is equal to 1 unit and 4 tenths. This means that the unit between 1 and 2 is divided into 10 equal parts, and 4 such parts are taken. Hence, 1.4 lies between 1 and 2. Draw the number line and divide the unit between 1 and 2 into 10 equal parts. Take the fourth part, and we have 1.4 on the number line.
Name all the divisions between 1 and 1.1 on the number line.
Identify and write the decimal numbers against the letters.

content.text:
Worked example: Locate 1.4 on the number line. Then name all the divisions between 1 and 1.1.
1. 1.4 is 1 unit and 4 tenths, so it lies between 1 and 2.
2. Split the unit from 1 to 2 into 10 equal parts: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and so on, and take the 4th part to reach 1.4.
3. Between 1 and 1.1 split the gap into 10 equal parts as well; each part is 1 hundredth.
4. The divisions are 1.01, 1.02, 1.03, 1.04, 1.05, 1.06, 1.07, 1.08 and 1.09.
Answer: 1.4 is the 4th mark after 1; the divisions are 1.01 to 1.09

concepts.concept_name: Tenths and hundredths on the number line

content.text:
Worked example: A line has large marks at 5, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4, with 10 small marks between neighbouring large marks. The letter A is 9 small marks after 5, B is 3 small marks after 5.1, C is on the large mark 5.2 and D is 1 small mark after 5.3. Read the decimal at each letter.
1. Large marks are tenths: 5, 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4.
2. Ten small marks fill a tenth, so each small mark is one hundredth.
3. A is 9 small marks after 5: 5 + 0.09 = 5.09.
4. B is 3 small marks after 5.1: 5.1 + 0.03 = 5.13.
5. C is on the large mark 5.2.
6. D is 1 small mark after 5.3: 5.3 + 0.01 = 5.31.
Answer: A = 5.09, B = 5.13, C = 5.2, D = 5.31

content.text:
Worked example: Locate 4.185 by zooming. Then read the decimal marked '?' in a zoom that goes from 3 to 4, then 3.0 to 3.1, then 3.05 to 3.06, and ends at the 9th mark of the last gap of 10 parts.
1. 4.185: the units digit 4 gives the gap 4 to 5. The tenths digit 1 gives 4.1 to 4.2. The hundredths digit 8 gives 4.18 to 4.19. The thousandths digit 5 gives the middle mark, 4.185.
2. '?': the first zoom is 3 to 4, so units 3. The second zoom is 3.0 to 3.1, so tenths 0. The third zoom is 3.05 to 3.06, so hundredths 5. The mark is the 9th part after 3.05 in a gap of 10 parts.
3. 9 thousandths more than 3.05, so the decimal is 3.059.
Answer: 4.185 is the middle mark of 4.18 to 4.19; '?' is 3.059

content.text:
1. Predict first: a line from 5 to 10 is cut into 10 equal parts. Is each part one tenth?
2. No. The length is 5 units, so each part is 5 divided by 10, which is half a unit.
3. Always find the value of one division first: the length of the line divided by the number of parts.

content.text:
Worked example: On a line from 5 to 10 cut into 10 equal parts, the box b is at the 5th division, a is at the 2nd division and c is at the 9th. Find the decimals.
1. The line is 10 − 5 = 5 units long, in 10 equal parts, so each part is 0.5.
2. b: 5 parts after 5 is 5 + 5 × 0.5 = 7.5.
3. a: 2 parts after 5 is 5 + 2 × 0.5 = 6.
4. c: 9 parts after 5 is 5 + 9 × 0.5 = 9.5.
Answer: a = 6, b = 7.5, c = 9.5

content.text:
Worked example: One line runs from 8 to 8.1 and is cut into 10 equal parts, with d at the 1st mark and e at the 5th. Another line starts at 4.3 and has marks every 0.05, with 4.8 at the 10th mark. The letter f is at the 1st mark, g is at the 4th mark and h is one mark past the 4.8 label. Find d, e, f, g and h.
1. Line 8 to 8.1: it is 0.1 long in 10 parts, so each part is 0.01. d is 8.01 and e is 8.05.
2. Line from 4.3: 10 marks of 0.05 reach 4.3 + 0.5 = 4.8, which fits the label.
3. f: 1 mark after 4.3 is 4.3 + 0.05 = 4.35.
4. g: 4 marks after 4.3 is 4.3 + 0.20 = 4.5.
5. h: one mark past 4.8 is 4.8 + 0.05 = 4.85.
Answer: d = 8.01, e = 8.05, f = 4.35, g = 4.5, h = 4.85

Answer: d = 8.01, e = 8.05, f = 4.35, g = 4.5, h = 4.85
content.question: One line runs from 8 to 8.1 and is cut into 10 equal parts, with d at the 1st mark and e at the 5th. Another line starts at 4.3 and has marks every 0.05, with 4.8 at the 10th mark. The letter f is at the 1st mark, g is at the 4th mark and h is one mark past the 4.8 label. Find d, e, f, g and h.
steps: Line 8 to 8.1: it is 0.1 long in 10 parts, so each part is 0.01. d is 8.01 and e is 8.05.
Line from 4.3: 10 marks of 0.05 reach 4.3 + 0.5 = 4.8, which fits the label.
g: 4 marks after 4.3 is 4.3 + 0.20 = 4.5.
h: one mark past 4.8 is 4.8 + 0.05 = 4.85.

concepts.concept_name: Practice: locate and read decimals on a number line

content.text:
Each digit gives one zoom into one of ten equal parts.
Find the value of one division first: the length of the line divided by the number of parts.
Read the end marks of the last zoom to name the decimal.

tool_config.title: Digit by Digit Zoom Locator
tool_config.idea: Every digit of a decimal names one more zoom: the units digit picks a gap between two whole numbers, the tenths digit picks one of 10 equal parts of that gap, the hundredths digit picks one part of that part, and so on, so any decimal has its own place on the number line.
tool_config.screen: A number line from 0 to 10 with a zoom window; each zoom opens the chosen gap into 10 equal parts and shows the new end marks; a decimal card with its digits lit one at a time; a stack of the lines already visited; a second mode where the student reads a marked point on a given line.
student_does: Read the first digit and zoom into that gap.
Read the next digit and zoom into that tenth of the gap.
Keep zooming until every digit is used, then place the marker.
Switch to a given line and read the decimal at a marked point.
challenges: A point on the line from 5 to 10 that sits 5 parts after 5, with every part half a unit (7.5).
A point 5 parts after 8 on the line from 8 to 8.1 (8.05).
A point on the line from 4.3 to 4.8 that sits 1 part after 4.8 when each part is 0.05 (4.85).
feedback: A digit zoomed into the wrong gap is shown by the end marks of the new line.
A line where the parts are not tenths is flagged by dividing the end gap by the number of parts.
A reading that ignores the end marks of the line is checked by counting the parts again.
tool_config.done_when: Six decimals are located or read, each through its digit by digit zoom.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q3: What decimal number does each letter represent in the number line? The line runs from 6.4 to 6.6, with marks every 0.025 between them. The point a is at the 2nd mark after 6.4, the point c is at the 5th mark and the point b is at the 6th mark.
1. The line runs from 6.4 to 6.6, which is 0.2 long, with 8 equal parts.
2. Each mark is 0.2 ÷ 8 = 0.025 apart.
3. a: 2 marks after 6.4 is 6.4 + 2 × 0.025 = 6.45.
4. c: 5 marks after 6.4 is 6.4 + 5 × 0.025 = 6.525.
5. b: 6 marks after 6.4 is 6.4 + 6 × 0.025 = 6.55.
Answer: a = 6.45, c = 6.525, b = 6.55

concepts.concept_name: The zero dilemma

content.text:
There is Zero Dilemma!
Sonu says that 0.2 can also be written as 0.20, 0.200; Zara thinks that putting zeros on the right side may alter the value of the decimal number. What do you think?
We can figure this out by looking at the quantities these numbers represent using place value.
We can see that 0.2, 0.20, and 0.200 are all equal as they represent the same quantity, i.e., 2 tenths. But 0.2, 0.02, and 0.002 are different.
Can you tell which of these is the smallest and which is the largest?
Which of these are the same: 4.5, 4.05, 0.405, 4.050, 4.50, 4.005, 04.50?

content.text:
1. Predict first: Sonu says 0.2 equals 0.20 and 0.200. Zara says extra zeroes may change the value. Who is right?
2. Put each in a place table. 0.2 is 2 tenths. 0.20 is 2 tenths and 0 hundredths. 0.200 adds 0 thousandths. All three are 2 tenths.
3. A zero at the far right adds nothing. A zero between the point and a digit changes everything: 0.02 is 2 hundredths.

content.text:
Worked example: Use a place table to settle Sonu and Zara, and then say which of 0.2, 0.20, 0.200, 0.02 and 0.002 is smallest and largest.
1. 0.2: units 0, tenths 2. 0.20: tenths 2, hundredths 0. 0.200: tenths 2, hundredths 0, thousandths 0.
2. All three show 2 tenths, so Sonu is right: they are equal.
3. 0.02 is 2 hundredths and 0.002 is 2 thousandths, which are different quantities.
4. 2 tenths is the most, then 2 hundredths, then 2 thousandths: the largest is 0.2 (= 0.20 = 0.200) and the smallest is 0.002.
Answer: 0.2, 0.20 and 0.200 are equal; the smallest is 0.002

concepts.concept_name: The zero dilemma

content.text:
Worked example: Which of these are the same: 4.5, 4.05, 0.405, 4.050, 4.50, 4.005, 04.50?
1. Strip zeroes from the right end of the decimal part and from the left end of the whole part.
2. 4.50 is 4.5 and 04.50 is 4.5, so 4.5, 4.50 and 04.50 are equal.
3. 4.050 is 4.05, so 4.05 and 4.050 are equal.
4. 0.405 and 4.005 are different from all of these.
Answer: 4.5 = 4.50 = 04.50, and 4.05 = 4.050; 0.405 and 4.005 stand alone

concepts.concept_name: Comparing place by place

content.text:
Which is larger: 6.456 or 6.465?
To answer this, we can use the number line to locate both decimal numbers and show which is larger. This can also be done by comparing the corresponding digits at each place value, as we do with whole numbers. This comparison is visualised step by step below.
Both numbers have 6 units. Both numbers have 6 units and 4 tenths. Both numbers have 6 units and 4 tenths, but the first number has only 5 hundredths, whereas the second number has 6 hundredths.
We start by comparing the most significant digits (digits with the highest place value) of the two numbers. If the digits are the same, we compare the next smaller place value. We keep going till we find a position where the digits are not equal. The number with the larger digit at this position is the greater of the two.
Why can we stop comparing at this point? Can we be sure that whatever digits are there after this will not affect our conclusion?
Which decimal number is greater? (a) 1.23 or 1.32 (b) 3.81 or 13.800 (c) 1.009 or 1.090

2. Start from the biggest place. Both have 6 units, and both have 4 tenths. At the hundredths, 5 is less than 6.

content.text:
Worked example: Which is larger, 6.456 or 6.465? Compare step by step and say why we can stop.
1. Units: 6 and 6, equal. Tenths: 4 and 4, equal.
2. Hundredths: 5 and 6, and 6 is greater, so 6.465 is the greater number.
3. Why stop: the digits after the hundredths place together are less than 1 hundredth. So the first number can gain at most just under one more hundredth, and the second is already one hundredth ahead.
Answer: 6.465 is larger

content.text:
Worked example: Which is greater? (a) 1.23 or 1.32 (b) 3.81 or 13.800 (c) 1.009 or 1.090
1. (a) Units equal. Tenths: 2 and 3, so 1.32 is greater.
2. (b) Tens: 3.81 has 0 tens and 13.800 has 1 ten, so 13.800 is greater, though it has a zero at the end.
3. (c) Units equal, tenths equal at 0. Hundredths: 0 and 9, so 1.090 is greater.
Answer: (a) 1.32 (b) 13.800 (c) 1.090

concepts.concept_name: Closest decimals

content.text:
Closest Decimals
Consider the decimal numbers 0.9, 1.1, 1.01, and 1.11. Identify the decimal number that is closest to 1.
Let us compare the decimal numbers. Arranging these in ascending order, we get 0.9 < 1 < 1.01 < 1.1 < 1.11. Among the neighbours of 1, 1.01 is 1/100 away from 1 whereas 0.9 is 10/100 away from 1. Therefore, 1.01 is closest to 1.
Which of the above is closest to 1.09?
Which among these is closest to 4: 3.56, 3.65, 3.099?
Which among these is closest to 1: 0.8, 0.69, 1.08?
In each case below use the digits 4, 1, 8, 2, and 5 exactly once and try to make a decimal number as close as possible to 25.

content.text:
Worked example: Which of 0.9, 1.1, 1.01 and 1.11 is closest to 1? Then which is closest to 1.09?
1. Gaps from 1: 0.9 is 0.1 away, 1.1 is 0.1 away, 1.01 is 0.01 away, and 1.11 is 0.11 away. So 1.01 is closest.
2. Gaps from 1.09: 0.9 is 0.19, 1.1 is 0.01, 1.01 is 0.08, and 1.11 is 0.02.
3. The smallest gap is 0.01, so 1.1 is closest to 1.09.
Answer: 1.01 is closest to 1; 1.1 is closest to 1.09

concepts.concept_name: Closest decimals

content.text:
Worked example: Use the digits 4, 1, 8, 2 and 5 exactly once each to make a decimal as close as possible to 25, with the point placed in different places.
1. With the point after one digit, such as 8.5421, the number is far from 25.
2. With the point after two digits, the tens and units can be 2 and 5: 25.148, which is 0.148 from 25.
3. With the point after three digits, such as 124.58, the number is far too big.
4. The best layout puts 2 and 5 as tens and units, then the smallest digits after the point: the remaining digits 1, 4 and 8 in order give 25.148.
Answer: 25.148 is the closest, 0.148 away

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students decide whether zeroes written at the right end of a decimal change its value, using a place value table, and tell which decimals among a group are equal.
Students compare two decimals digit by digit from the biggest place, stop at the first place where the digits differ, and explain why the later digits cannot change the answer.
Students find the decimal nearest to a target by comparing the size of each gap, and use a set of digits to make a decimal as close as possible to a target.
Students compare and order decimals place by place and find the decimal closest to a number.

content.book_number: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q4
content.question: Arrange the following quantities in descending order: (a) 11.01, 1.011, 1.101, 11.10, 1.01 (b) 2.567, 2.675, 2.768, 2.499, 2.698 (c) 4.678 g, 4.595 g, 4.600 g, 4.656 g, 4.666 g (d) 33.13 m, 33.31 m, 33.133 m, 33.331 m, 33.313 m
steps: (a) Write with 3 decimal places: 11.010, 1.011, 1.101, 11.100, 1.010. The tens digit puts 11.100 and 11.010 first, then 1.101, 1.011 and 1.010.
(b) Tenths: 5, 6, 7, 4, 6. So 2.768 first and 2.499 last; of the 6s, 2.698 is above 2.675; of the 5s, only 2.567.
(c) Hundredths decide: 4.678 g, 4.666 g, 4.656 g, 4.600 g, 4.595 g.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q5

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q5: Using the digits 1, 4, 0, 8, and 6 make: (a) the decimal number closest to 30 (b) the smallest possible decimal number between 100 and 1000.
1. (a) A number close to 30 needs its tens and units digits close to 30. The digits 1, 4, 0, 8, 6 cannot make 3, so try the tens digit 4 with the smallest digits after it: 40.168, which is 10.168 away.
2. Other tries are farther: 18.046 is 11.954 below 30, and 61.048 is 31.048 above 30.
3. (b) Between 100 and 1000 means 3 whole digits. The smallest puts the smallest non-zero digit first, 1, then 0, then 4, then the rest in order: 104.68.
Answer: (a) 40.168 (b) 104.68

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q6

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q6: Will a decimal number with more digits be greater than a decimal number with fewer digits?
1. Try 2.05 and 2.5. The first has more digits after the point.
2. Tenths: 0 and 5, so 2.5 is greater.
3. So the number of digits does not decide, and the answer is no.
Answer: No. For example 2.5 is greater than 2.05, though 2.05 has more digits

content.text:
3.7 Addition and Subtraction of Decimals
Priya requires 2.7 m of cloth for her skirt, and Shylaja requires 3.5m for her kurti. What is the total quantity of cloth needed? We have to find the sum of 2.7m + 3.5m.
Earlier, we saw how to add 2 7/10 + 3 5/10 (also shown below). Can you carry out the same addition using decimal notation? It is shown below. Share your observations. The total quantity of cloth needed is 6.2 m.
As you can see, the standard procedure for adding and subtracting whole numbers can be used to add and subtract decimals.
A detailed view of the underlying place value calculation is shown below for the sum 75.345 + 86.691. Its compact form is shown next to it.

content.text:
Worked example: Priya needs 2.7 m of cloth and Shylaja needs 3.5 m. How much cloth is needed in all? Compare with adding 2 7/10 and 3 5/10.
1. Write the numbers with the points in one line: 2.7 above 3.5.
2. Tenths: 7 + 5 = 12 tenths, which is 1 unit and 2 tenths. Write 2 and carry 1.
3. Units: 2 + 3 + 1 carried = 6. The point stays between the 6 and the 2.
4. In fractions, 2 7/10 + 3 5/10 = 5 12/10 = 6 2/10, which is 6.2 again.
Answer: 6.2 m

content.text:
Worked example: Add 75.345 and 86.691 in the compact form, and say what each carry means.
1. Line up the points: 75.345 above 86.691.
2. Thousandths: 5 + 1 = 6. Hundredths: 4 + 9 = 13, so write 3 and carry 1 to the tenths.
3. Tenths: 3 + 6 + 1 = 10, so write 0 and carry 1 to the units. Units: 5 + 6 + 1 = 12, so write 2 and carry 1 to the tens.
4. Tens: 7 + 8 + 1 = 16, so write 6 and carry 1 to the hundreds. Hundreds: 1.
5. The sum is 162.036.
Answer: 162.036

concepts.concept_name: Estimating a sum first

content.text:
Estimating Sums and Differences
Sonu has observed sums and differences of decimal numbers and says, “If we add two decimal numbers, then the sum will always be greater than the sum of their whole number parts. Also, the sum will always be less than 2 more than the sum of their whole number parts.”
Let us use an example to understand what his claim means: If the two numbers to be added are 25.936 and 8.202, the claim is that their sum will be greater than 25 + 8 (whole number parts) and will be less than 25 + 1 + 8 + 1.
What do you think about this claim? Verify if this is true for these numbers. Will it work for any 2 decimal numbers? What about for the sum of 25.93603259 and 8.202?
Note to the Teacher: Estimating the result before computing may help in identifying if a mistake happens with the calculation.

Worked example: Check Sonu's claim for 25.936 and 8.202, and for 25.93603259 and 8.202.
1. Whole parts: 25 and 8, total 33. The range from the claim is 33 to 35.
2. 25.936 + 8.202 = 34.138. It is above 33 and below 35, so the claim holds.
3. 25.93603259 + 8.202 = 34.13803259, which also lies between 33 and 35.
4. Each fractional part is under 1, so two of them together are under 2. That is why the sum stays under the whole parts total plus 2.
5. The sum equals the whole parts total only when both fractional parts are zero, such as 5.0 and 3.0, so 'greater than' should really read 'greater than or equal to'.
Answer: 34.138 and 34.13803259 both lie between 33 and 35; the claim holds for any two decimals, with 'equal to' allowed at the low end

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (adding and subtracting decimals), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (adding and subtracting decimals), Q1: Find the sums: (a) 5.3 + 2.6 (b) 18 + 8.8 (c) 2.15 + 5.26 (d) 9.01 + 9.10 (e) 29.19 + 9.91 (f) 0.934 + 0.6 (g) 0.75 + 0.03 (h) 6.236 + 0.487
1. (a) Tenths: 3 + 6 = 9. Units: 5 + 2 = 7. So 7.9.
2. (b) Write 18 as 18.0. Tenths: 0 + 8 = 8. Units: 8 + 8 = 16, so 26.8.
3. (c) Hundredths: 5 + 6 = 11, write 1 and carry 1. Tenths: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. Units: 2 + 5 = 7. So 7.41.
4. (d) Hundredths: 1 + 0 = 1. Tenths: 0 + 1 = 1. Units: 9 + 9 = 18. So 18.11.
5. (e) Hundredths: 9 + 1 = 10, write 0 and carry 1. Tenths: 1 + 9 + 1 = 11, write 1 and carry 1. Units: 9 + 9 + 1 = 19, write 9 and carry 1. Tens: 2 + 1 = 3 and 1. So 39.10.
6. (f) Write 0.6 as 0.600. Thousandths: 4. Hundredths: 3. Tenths: 9 + 6 = 15, write 5 and carry 1. Units: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. So 1.534.
7. (g) Write 0.03 as 0.03. Hundredths: 5 + 3 = 8. Tenths: 7. So 0.78.
8. (h) Thousandths: 6 + 7 = 13, write 3 and carry 1. Hundredths: 3 + 8 + 1 = 12, write 2 and carry 1. Tenths: 2 + 4 + 1 = 7. Units: 6. So 6.723.
Answer: (a) 7.9 (b) 26.8 (c) 7.41 (d) 18.11 (e) 39.10 (f) 1.534 (g) 0.78 (h) 6.723

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q7: Mahi purchases 0.25 kg of beans, 0.3 kg of carrots, 0.5 kg of potatoes, 0.2 kg of capsicums, and 0.05 kg of ginger. Calculate the total weight of the items she bought.
1. Write each with two places: 0.25, 0.30, 0.50, 0.20 and 0.05.
2. Hundredths: 5 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 5 = 10, write 0 and carry 1 to the tenths.
3. Tenths: 2 + 3 + 5 + 2 + 1 carried = 13, write 3 and carry 1 to the units.
4. Units: 1. The total is 1.30 kg.
Answer: 1.3 kg

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q15

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q15: Using each digit 0 to 9 not more than once, fill the boxes of a sum of two decimals, each with one digit before the point and three digits after it, so that the sum is closest to 10.5.
1. Each number is a digit, a point and three more digits, so eight different digits are used.
2. Aim for a sum of exactly 10.500. The thousandths digits must add to 10, and every other place must add to make the right sum with a carry.
3. Try 0.643 + 9.857: thousandths 3 + 7 = 10, hundredths 4 + 5 + 1 = 10, tenths 6 + 8 + 1 = 15, units 0 + 9 + 1 = 10.
4. The sum is 10.500 and the eight digits 0, 6, 4, 3, 9, 8, 5, 7 are all different, so the gap from 10.5 is zero.
Answer: 0.643 + 9.857 is exactly 10.500

content.text:
Worked example: Shylaja needs 3.5 m of cloth and Priya needs 2.7 m. How much longer is Shylaja's cloth? Compare with 3 5/10 − 2 7/10.
1. Line up the points: 3.5 above 2.7.
2. Tenths: 5 is less than 7, so borrow 1 unit from the 3. The 3 becomes 2 and the 5 tenths become 15 tenths.
3. 15 − 7 = 8 tenths. Units: 2 − 2 = 0. So the difference is 0.8.
4. In fractions, 3 5/10 − 2 7/10 = 2 15/10 − 2 7/10 = 0 8/10, which is 0.8 again.
Answer: 0.8 m

content.text:
Worked example: Find 84.691 − 77.345 in the place value form and in the compact form.
1. Line up the points: 84.691 above 77.345.
2. Thousandths: 1 is less than 5, so borrow 1 hundredth: 11 − 5 = 6, and the hundredths 9 become 8.
3. Hundredths: 8 − 4 = 4. Tenths: 6 − 3 = 3.
4. Units: 4 is less than 7, so borrow 1 ten: 14 − 7 = 7, and the tens 8 become 7. Tens: 7 − 7 = 0.
5. The difference is 7.346.
Answer: 7.346

content.text:
1. Predict first: for 8.9 minus 3.1, what is the least and what is the most the answer could be?
2. Each decimal is its whole part plus a fraction under 1. The difference of the whole parts is the base, and the fractions can move it up or down by less than 1.
3. So the difference lies between the whole parts difference minus 1 and the whole parts difference plus 1.

content.text:
Worked example: Find a range for 84.691 − 77.345 and for 5.2 − 4.9, from the whole number parts, then check.
1. 84.691 and 77.345 have whole parts 84 and 77, whose difference is 7. The range is from 6 to 8.
2. The actual difference is 7.346, which lies between 6 and 8.
3. 5.2 and 4.9 have whole parts 5 and 4, whose difference is 1. The range is from 0 to 2.
4. The actual difference is 0.3, which lies between 0 and 2.
5. Each fractional part is under 1, so their difference is more than −1 and less than 1. That is why the range is the whole parts difference with 1 taken off and added.
Answer: The difference lies between the whole parts difference minus 1 and plus 1: 7.346 is between 6 and 8, 0.3 is between 0 and 2

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (adding and subtracting decimals), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (adding and subtracting decimals), Q2: Find the differences: (a) 5.6 − 2.3 (b) 18 − 8.8 (c) 10.4 − 4.5 (d) 17 − 16.198 (e) 17 − 0.05 (f) 34.505 − 18.1 (g) 9.9 − 9.09 (h) 6.236 − 0.487
1. (a) Tenths: 6 − 3 = 3. Units: 5 − 2 = 3. So 3.3.
2. (b) Write 18 as 18.0. Tenths: borrow, 10 − 8 = 2. Units: 17 − 8 = 9. So 9.2.
3. (c) Tenths: borrow, 14 − 5 = 9. Units: 9 − 4 = 5. So 5.9.
4. (d) Write 17 as 17.000. 17.000 − 16.198: the thousandths, hundredths and tenths all borrow, giving 0.802.
5. (e) Write 17 as 17.00. 17.00 − 0.05 = 16.95.
6. (f) Write 18.1 as 18.100. 34.505 − 18.100 = 16.405.
7. (g) Write 9.9 as 9.90. 9.90 − 9.09 = 0.81.
8. (h) 6.236 − 0.487: thousandths borrow, hundredths borrow, tenths borrow, giving 5.749.
Answer: (a) 3.3 (b) 9.2 (c) 5.9 (d) 0.802 (e) 16.95 (f) 16.405 (g) 0.81 (h) 5.749

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q8

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q8: Pinto supplies 3.79 L, 4.2 L, and 4.25 L of milk to a milk dairy in the first three days. In 6 days, he supplies 25 litres of milk. Find the total quantity of milk supplied to the dairy in the last three days.
1. First three days: 3.79 + 4.20 + 4.25. Hundredths: 9 + 0 + 5 = 14, write 4 and carry 1. Tenths: 7 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 12, write 2 and carry 1. Units: 3 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 12. The total is 12.24 L.
2. In 6 days he supplies 25 L, so the last three days are 25 − 12.24.
3. Write 25 as 25.00. 25.00 − 12.24 = 12.76.
Answer: 12.76 L

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q9

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q9: Tinku weighed 35.75 kg in January and 34.50 kg in February. Has he gained or lost weight? How much is the change?
1. February's weight 34.50 is less than January's 35.75, so he lost weight.
2. The change is 35.75 − 34.50. Hundredths: 5 − 0 = 5. Tenths: 7 − 5 = 2. Units: 5 − 4 = 1.
3. The change is 1.25 kg.
Answer: He has lost weight, 1.25 kg

concepts.concept_name: Finding the change and extending a decimal sequence

content.text:
Decimal Sequences
Observe this sequence of decimal numbers and identify the change after each term. 4.4, 4.8. 5.2, 5.6, 6.0, …
We can see that 0.4 is being added to a term to get the next term. Continue this sequence and write the next 3 terms.
Similarly, identify the change and write the next 3 terms for each sequence given below. Try to do this computation mentally. (a) 4.4, 4.45, 4.5, … (b) 25.75, 26.25, 26.75, … (c) 10.56, 10.67, 10.78, … (d) 13.5, 16, 18.5, … (e) 8.5, 9.4, 10.3, … (f) 5, 4.95, 4.90, … (g) 12.45, 11.95, 11.45, … (h) 36.5, 33, 29.5, …
Make your own sequences and challenge your classmates to extend the pattern.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in 4.4, 4.8, 5.2 the terms grow. By how much each time?
2. Subtract one term from the next. If the answer is the same each time, that is the change.
3. Add the change to get on, or subtract it if the terms fall.
4. Then make your own sequence, hide the next terms and challenge a classmate.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the change in 4.4, 4.8, 5.2, 5.6, 6.0 and write the next 3 terms.
1. 4.8 − 4.4 = 0.4, and 5.2 − 4.8 = 0.4, so 0.4 is added each time.
2. 6.0 + 0.4 = 6.4. 6.4 + 0.4 = 6.8. 6.8 + 0.4 = 7.2.
Answer: 6.4, 6.8, 7.2

content.text:
Figure it Out (end of chapter), Q10: Extend the pattern: 5.5, 6.4, 6.39, 7.29, 7.28, 8.18, 8.17, ____, ____
1. 6.4 − 5.5 = 0.9, so the first change is plus 0.9.
2. 6.39 is 0.01 less than 6.4, so the next change is minus 0.01.
3. 7.29 − 6.39 = 0.9 and 7.28 is 0.01 less than 7.29, so the changes alternate: plus 0.9, minus 0.01, plus 0.9, minus 0.01.
4. The last term shown is 8.17 after a minus 0.01, so the next change is plus 0.9: 9.07.
5. Then minus 0.01 gives 9.06.
Answer: 9.07, 9.06

concepts.concept_name: Decimal and measurement disasters

content.text:
3.8 More on the Decimal System
Decimal and Measurement Disasters
Decimal point and unit conversion mistakes may seem minor sometimes but they can lead to serious problems. Here are some actual incidents in which such errors caused major issues.
In 2013, the finance office of Amsterdam City Council (Netherlands) mistakenly sent out €188 million in housing benefits instead of the intended €1.8 million due to a programming error that processed payments in euro cents instead of euros. (1 euro-cent = 1/100 euro).
In 1983, a decimal error nearly caused a disaster for an Air Canada Boeing 767. The ground staff miscalculated the fuel, loading 22,300 pounds instead of kilograms, about half of what was needed (1 pound ~ 0.453 kg). The plane ran out of fuel mid-air, forcing the pilots to make an emergency landing at an abandoned airfield. Fortunately, everyone survived.
Several incidents have occurred due to incorrect reading of decimal numbers while giving medication. For example, reading 0.05 mg as 0.5 mg can lead to using a medicine 10 times more than the prescribed quantity. It is therefore important to pay attention to units and the location of the decimal point.

content.text:
Worked example: In 2013 a council meant to send 1.8 million euros but sent 188 million euros, because payments were processed in euro cents instead of euros. How many times larger was the amount sent? Also, why is 0.05 mg read as 0.5 mg a serious error?
1. 188 million divided by 1.8 million is about 104, so roughly 100 times larger. That matches the slip between cents and euros, where one euro-cent is 1/100 euro.
2. 0.05 mg is 5 hundredths of a mg. 0.5 mg is 5 tenths of a mg.
3. 5 tenths is 10 times 5 hundredths, so reading 0.05 as 0.5 gives a dose 10 times too big.
4. Always check the unit and the place of the decimal point.
Answer: About 100 times larger; the medicine dose would be 10 times larger

concepts.concept_name: Decimal and measurement disasters

content.text:
Worked example: A ground crew loaded 22300 pounds of fuel when 22300 kilograms was needed, and 1 pound is about 0.453 kg. About how many kilograms was loaded, and how does it compare with what was needed?
1. 22300 × 0.453 is about 10102 kg, found by multiplying the pounds by 0.453.
2. What was needed was 22300 kg.
3. 10102 is a little less than half of 22300, so the plane carried about half of the fuel it needed.
4. The unit slip, pounds for kilograms, is the same kind of error as a decimal slip.
Answer: About 10102 kg, about half of what was needed

concepts.concept_name: Numbers that look decimal but are not

content.text:
Deceptive Decimal Notation
Sarayu gets a message: “The bus will reach the station 4.5 hours post noon.” When will the bus reach the station: 4:05 p.m., 4:50 p.m., 4:25 p.m.?
None of these! Here, 0.5 hours means splitting an hour into 10 equal parts and taking 5 parts out of it. Each part will be 6 minutes (60 minutes/10) long. 5 such parts make 30 minutes. So, the bus will reach the station at 4:30.
Here is a short-story of a decimal mishap: A girl measures the width of an opening as 2 ft 5 inches but conveys to the carpenter to make a door 2.5 ft wide. The carpenter makes a door of width 2 ft 6 inches (since 1 ft = 12 inches, 0.5 ft = 6 inches), and it wouldn’t close fully.
If you watch cricket, you might have noticed decimal-looking numbers like ‘Overs left: 5.5’. Does this mean 5 overs and 5 balls or 5 overs and 3 balls? Here, 5.5 overs means 5 5/6 overs (as 1 over = 6 balls), i.e., 5 overs and 5 balls.
Where else can we see such ‘non-decimals’ with a decimal-like notation?

content.text:
Worked example: A message says the bus reaches at 4.5 hours post noon. When does it arrive? Then, a door was ordered 2.5 ft wide when the opening was 2 ft 5 inches. How wide did the carpenter make it?
1. 0.5 hours is 5 parts out of 10 equal parts of an hour. Each part is 60 ÷ 10 = 6 minutes.
2. 5 parts make 5 × 6 = 30 minutes, so the bus arrives at 4:30 p.m.
3. A foot is 12 inches, so 0.5 ft is half of 12 inches, that is 6 inches.
4. The carpenter made a door 2 ft 6 inches wide, 1 inch too wide for the opening, so it would not close fully.
Answer: 4:30 p.m.; the door was 2 ft 6 inches, 1 inch too wide

concepts.concept_name: Practice: spot the decimal mix-up

content.text:
Check the unit and the place of the decimal point before using a number.
A number with a point is a decimal only if each place is worth ten times the next.
Hours, feet and overs are not counted in tens.

concepts.concept_name: From India to the first decimal notation

content.text:
A Pinch of History: Decimal Notation Over Time
Decimal fractions (i.e., fractions with denominators like 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000, and so on) are used in the works of a number of ancient Indian astronomers and mathematicians, including in the important 8th century works of Śhrīdharāchārya on arithmetic and algebra.
Decimal notation, in essentially its modern form, was described in detail in Kitāb al-Fuṣūl fī al-Ḥisāb al Hindī (The Book of Chapters on Indian Arithmetic) by Abūl Ḥassan al-Uqlīdisī, an Arab mathematician, in around 950 CE. He represented the number 0.059375 with a small vertical mark placed after the zero that is the whole number part.
In the 15th century, to separate whole numbers from fractional parts, a number of different notations were used: a vertical mark on the last digit of the whole number part (as shown above), use of different colours and a numerical superscript giving the number of fractional decimal places (0.36 would be written as the digits 36 with a small 2 above them).

content.text:
Worked example: Order these events from earliest to latest: the 8th century works of Shridharacharya, the book of al-Uqlidisi around 950 CE, the 15th century notations, and the use of the point in the 16th century.
1. The 8th century is the 700s.
2. 950 CE is in the 900s, so it comes after the 8th century.
3. The 15th century is the 1400s, and the 16th century is the 1500s.
4. So the order is Shridharacharya, al-Uqlidisi, the 15th century marks, and the 16th century point.
Answer: 8th century, about 950 CE, 15th century, 16th century

concepts.concept_name: The point and the comma

content.text:
In the 16th century, John Napier, a Scottish mathematician, and Christopher Clavius, a German mathematician, used the point/period (‘.’) to separate the whole number and the fractional parts, while François Viète, a French mathematician, used the comma (‘,’) instead.
Currently, several countries use the comma to separate the integer part and the fractional part. In these countries, the number 1,000.5 is written with a space after the 1 and a comma before the 5 (space as a thousand separator). But the decimal point has endured as the most popular notation for writing numbers having fractional parts in the Indian place value system.
